<p class="mw-kicker">Marketing in 3 · Issue 5 · Week of 9 February 2026</p>
<figure class="mw-hero"><picture><source type="image/webp" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" srcset="../../images/web/issue-05-live-streaming-liveness-lift-960.webp 960w, ../../images/web/issue-05-live-streaming-liveness-lift-1600.webp 1600w"><img src="../../images/issue-05-live-streaming-liveness-lift.jpg" alt="A metal guitarist headbangs on a small club stage, long hair flying in a blur under red light, with another long-haired musician thrashing in the foreground" width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async"></picture><figcaption>Being there, even through a screen. Photo: Evgeniy Smersh on Unsplash.</figcaption></figure>
<section class="mw-answer" aria-label="Short answer"><h2>The short answer</h2><p>Often, yes. In five experiments with more than 3,000 viewers, simply believing a video was live, with nothing else changed, made people feel more present and more connected to the person on screen. They enjoyed it more, were more likely to keep watching and more willing to follow and subscribe. The lift was strongest when the person&#x27;s face was visible, and it did not depend on suspense. The studies used music streams; the authors expect the effect to be weaker when viewers only want information.</p></section>
<section class="mw-takeaways"><h2>Key takeaways</h2><ul><li>Told that an identical clip was live, viewers chose to keep watching it rather than switch to The Simpsons far more often (5.19 against 3.59 on a 1–7 scale).</li><li>Believing the stream was live raised the sense of &quot;being there&quot; (5.19 against 4.17), and that feeling explained the extra connection and engagement.</li><li>Show a face. When only the performer&#x27;s hands were visible, the live advantage for continued viewing disappeared (4.31 against 4.08).</li><li>Planned content worked as well as spontaneous content: the lift came from connection, not from suspense or surprise.</li></ul></section>
<section id="what-the-researchers-did"><h2>What the researchers did</h2><p>Live streaming is no longer a niche: viewers spent around 34 billion hours watching live streams in 2024, and
platforms such as Twitch, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram push creators and brands to go live. Meta paid more than
US$50 million to creators when it launched Facebook Live. But does live content work better than the same content
recorded, and if so, why?</p><p><a class="mw-orcid-link" href="https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9928-8336" title="Nofar Duani on ORCID">Nofar Duani</a> (University of Southern California), Alixandra Barasch (University of Colorado Boulder) and Adrian
Ward (University of Texas at Austin) tested this with amateur music performances. Viewers watched real Twitch
streams, a real band&#x27;s YouTube concert either live or the next day, and, in the tightest tests, the very same clip
of a singer presented as either live or recorded. Only the label changed: a live badge, the current date and a
progress bar that could not be skipped forward.</p>
<dl class="mw-facts"><div><dt>Experiments</dt><dd>5 online experiments with 3,034 viewers, 395 to 945 each</dd></div><div><dt>Platforms</dt><dd>Twitch&#x27;s music channel, a live YouTube concert by the band Sunny and the Black Pack, and a purpose-built streaming page</dd></div><div><dt>Measures</dt><dd>Sense of presence, connection to the performer and to other viewers, enjoyment, choice to keep watching, and willingness to follow, subscribe and join the fan community</dd></div><div><dt>Open data</dt><dd>Data, code, materials and preregistrations on OSF</dd></div></dl>
</section>
<section id="what-they-found"><h2>What they found</h2><p>Liveness itself made a difference. On Twitch, people who watched a live stream felt more connected (56.7 against
49.6 out of 100) and enjoyed it more (48.8 against 43.5) than people choosing among the same channel&#x27;s recorded
streams. With the band&#x27;s identical concert, the live audience enjoyed it more (57.2 against 51.8).</p><p>When everything except the word &quot;live&quot; was held constant, the effects grew. Viewers who thought the clip was live
felt more present in the scene, closer to the singer, and more willing to watch more of her videos, follow her on
social media, subscribe and join her fan community. Offered the choice of two more minutes of the same video or a
clip from The Simpsons, they were far more likely to stay.</p>

<section id="why-live-feels-different"><h2>Why live feels different</h2><p>For most of human history, seeing something as it happened meant being there. The authors argue that this link
is so ingrained that watching in real time makes people feel present in the scene, and feeling present with
someone makes people feel connected to them, much as strangers bond by sharing a moment in the same room.</p><p>The data back this chain: knowing the stream was live raised presence, presence raised connection to the
performer, and connection drove enjoyment, continued viewing and following. It was not about suspense. Telling
viewers that the band&#x27;s set was planned in advance, rather than spontaneous, did not remove the lift.</p>
</section>
<section id="show-a-face"><h2>Show a face</h2><p>The lift depends on seeing the person. When viewers saw the singer&#x27;s face, believing the video was live made them
much more likely to keep watching (4.89 against 3.69). When the same song played over a shot of only the
musician&#x27;s hands on a keyboard, liveness made almost no difference (4.31 against 4.08). A face gives viewers enough
of the scene to feel they are in it.</p>

<section id="bigger-audiences-are-not-more-intimate"><h2>Bigger audiences are not more intimate</h2><p>Viewer counters can backfire. Varying the &quot;watching now&quot; counter from 0 to about 1,000 did not change the live
advantage, which held at every audience size, but people felt closest to the performer and most willing to follow
when they thought they were watching alone or with few others. A large visible crowd made the experience feel
less personal.</p><p>Other viewers matter in a different way. When the band streamed on YouTube with a live chat and viewer count, live
viewers felt much more connected to the other viewers (41.1 against 28.7 out of 100), and that sense of community
also drove enjoyment and intention to follow.</p>

<section id="how-to-apply-it" class="mw-howto"><p class="mw-rsg-kicker">Marketing in 3 steps</p><h2>Ready. Set. Market.</h2><div class="mw-rsg"><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">1</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Ready</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Decide and prepare</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Go live for moments that build relationships.</strong> Product launches, behind-the-scenes sessions, founder or expert Q&amp;As, live shopping and community events are where connection matters most. The studies suggest a recording of the same session will not create the same pull.</li><li><strong>Plan freely.</strong> A rehearsed, scripted live session still produced the lift. You do not need risky improvisation; you need real time and a visible human.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">2</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Set</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Build it</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Make liveness obvious.</strong> The lift came from believing the stream was live. Use the platform&#x27;s live badge, say the date and time on screen, refer to what is happening now, and avoid formats that look edited.</li><li><strong>Keep a person on camera.</strong> Put the host&#x27;s face in view throughout. For demos, slides or gameplay, use picture-in-picture so viewers can see the presenter&#x27;s reactions alongside the product.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">3</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Market</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Launch and measure</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Think twice about big viewer counters.</strong> Show audience numbers when you want a sense of community, but do not expect a large crowd to make people feel closer to the host. Small, intimate sessions can engage more.</li><li><strong>Test live against recorded.</strong> Run the same content live and as a recording and compare watch time, follows, sign-ups or sales. Expect a smaller lift for how-to and training content, where viewers mainly want information.</li></ul></div></div></section>

<section id="what-to-expect"><h2>What to expect</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>More viewers who stay.</strong> Continued viewing was the clearest effect: 5.19 against 3.59 out of 7 when only the live label differed.</li><li><strong>More follows and subscriptions.</strong> Willingness to watch more, follow, subscribe and join a fan community rose by about 0.8 points out of 7.</li><li><strong>Modest enjoyment gains in the wild.</strong> On real platforms, enjoyment rose by about 5 points out of 100, and the effect on following the real band was only marginal.</li><li><strong>Little extra cost.</strong> The effect came from the content being live, not from bigger production budgets; the authors suggest that heavy polish may even reduce the intimacy that drives it.</li></ul></section>
<section id="where-it-does-not-work"><h2>Where it does not work</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>Music only.</strong> All five experiments used amateur music performances. Effects for product demos, webinars, live shopping or corporate events are expected but untested.</li><li><strong>Information-seekers may not care.</strong> The authors caution that viewers of how-to, cooking or training streams who mainly want skills may get less of the lift.</li><li><strong>Amateur, not polished.</strong> It is unknown whether highly produced or celebrity streams benefit in the same way.</li><li><strong>Short clips, self-reports.</strong> Viewers watched one to a few minutes, and presence and connection were self-reported; continued viewing was a real but short-term choice.</li></ul></section>
<section id="questions"><h2>Questions marketers ask</h2><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Is live video more engaging than recorded video?</h3><p>Yes, in a Journal of Marketing study. When viewers were told an identical clip was live rather than recorded, they felt more connected to the person on screen, were more likely to keep watching (5.19 against 3.59 out of 7) and more willing to follow and subscribe (<a class="mw-orcid-link" href="https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9928-8336" title="Nofar Duani on ORCID">Duani</a> et al., 2026).</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Why do people prefer live streams?</h3><p>Watching something as it happens makes people feel they are there. That sense of presence makes them feel connected to the person on screen, and connection drives enjoyment, continued viewing and following. The effect did not depend on suspense or spontaneity.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Should brands use live streaming?</h3><p>For content where connection matters, such as launches, behind-the-scenes sessions, Q&amp;As and live shopping, the evidence favours going live with a visible host. The research used music streams, so brands should test live against recorded versions of their own content.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Does showing the presenter&#x27;s face matter in live video?</h3><p>Yes. When viewers could see a performer&#x27;s face, liveness clearly increased continued viewing (4.89 against 3.69 out of 7). When only the performer&#x27;s hands were shown, the live advantage disappeared (4.31 against 4.08).</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Do bigger live audiences increase engagement?</h3><p>Not with the host. The live advantage held for audiences of 0 to about 1,000, but viewers felt closest to the performer and most willing to follow when they believed few others were watching.</p></div></section>
<section id="also-new"><h2>Also new this week</h2><div class="mw-also"><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>Journal of Interactive Marketing</em> · 2026</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10949968261425234">Selling together: A signaling perspective on co-livestreaming effectiveness</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Yang, Z., Zhang, L., Cao, X., &amp; Lu, H.</p><p>Livestreams in which an influencer sells alongside a brand representative brought more sales and more new followers than influencer-only streams, in sales data and three experiments. A brand rep on screen signals that the brand stands behind the influencer, which makes the influencer more credible. The benefit shrinks when the influencer or the brand is already very popular, so co-streaming pays most for smaller names.</p></article><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>European Journal of Marketing</em> · 2026</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/ejm-09-2024-0783">When the thrill lingers: How post-purchase flow consciousness shapes live-stream shopping engagement</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Yuan, D.-H., Deng, R., &amp; Lin, Z.</p><p>Shoppers who look back on a live-stream purchase and recognise how absorbed they were feel less regret, enjoy the purchase more and engage more with the seller afterwards, across an experiment, a survey and a second experiment. The effect was stronger under strict return policies. Follow-up messages that remind buyers of the fun of the stream can protect against buyer&#x27;s remorse.</p></article></div></section>
